new_statements.quote: Por otra parte, en palabras bisílabas el acento de intensidad se asocia a la sílaba que presenta el tono H, pero cuando no presenta tono H el acento se asocia a la primera sílaba a la izquierda. En la realización de palabras compuestas bisílabas más cohesionados o lexicalizados el tono H coocurre con el acento en la primera sílaba. [p.217] [...] La realización del tono y el acento en la mayoría de las palabras bisílabas y en las trisílabas monomorfémicas en la primera sílaba, se podría interpretar como un acento fijo y sin carácter contrastivo. [p.233]
new_statements.translation: On the other hand, in bisyllabic words intensity stress is associated with the syllable that carries the H tone, but when there is no H tone the stress is associated with the first syllable from the left. In the realization of more cohesive or lexicalized bisyllabic compounds the H tone co-occurs with the stress on the first syllable. [...] The realization of tone and stress on the first syllable in most bisyllabic and in trisyllabic monomorphemic words could be interpreted as a fixed, non-contrastive stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mixed 'tono acentual' system: three contrastive tones (L default, HL, LH) on monosyllabic lexemes (nouns, adjectives, verbs, pronouns, some deictics and TAM markers); each morpheme has at most one H. Intensity stress is predictable, not contrastive: it falls on the syllable bearing H tone, and on the first syllable when the word has no H; since H is almost always on the first syllable of bi/trisyllabic monomorphemic words (patterns H.L, H.L.L, L.L, L.L.L all stressed initially), stress is in effect word-initial, 'stress to high tone' attracting stress leftward (Wetzels & Meira). Stress delimits the prosodic word and distinguishes more from less lexicalized compounds (p.237).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; each morpheme carries at most one H tone; polymorphemic compounds may keep two prosodic words or lose one constituent's tone (§4.5.3).
new_statements.exceptions: Few L.H bisyllables (e.g. /ba'ɹúʔ/ 'perro', /pu'iúʔ/ 'algodón silvestre') and L.H.L trisyllables (/pɤ'pere/, /~ka'búkɤ/) carry H and stress on the second syllable; the author notes these are mostly loans (Arawak, Eastern Tukanoan) or opaque compounds; two L.H.L words keep the intensity peak on the first syllable while the H stays on the second (p.233).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: monomorphemic bisyllabic and trisyllabic words and compounds, elicited in isolation and measured in Praat (F0 in Hz, intensity, duration); the phonetic transcription marks stress with ' before the stressed syllable in bi/trisyllabic monomorphemic words (p.166). Tone has no grammatical function (p.218).
new_statements.identity_note: Mahecha 2024 describes Nɨkak (Nukak) proper (nuka1242, ISO mbr) as spoken in Guaviare, Colombia (~950 speakers); data from several local groups (dialect variation in lexicon noted, not in stress). Not the sister language Kakua (cacu1241).

sources.note: Ch.4 (Fonología), §4.5 'Tono y acento en la lengua Nɨkak' pp.217-239: mixed system ('tono acentual', 'stress to high tone'); three contrastive tones L/HL/LH in monosyllabic lexemes; in bisyllables intensity stress goes to the H-tone syllable, otherwise to the first syllable from the left; most bi/trisyllabic monomorphemic words have H+stress on the first syllable, 'se podría interpretar como un acento fijo y sin carácter contrastivo' (p.233); stress 'es previsible y tiene la función de delimitar la palabra prosódica' (p.237). Praat measurements.
